title: Test a capacitor
summary: Spot failed capacitors by eye, discharge them safely, and check their value and leakage with a meter. Covers small electrolytics on circuit boards and the motor run and start capacitors that kill air conditioners, pumps and fans.

steps.text: Discharge the capacitor with a resistor tool and check it on DC volts before touching it.
steps.warn: Never test a capacitor that might be charged. Follow the capacitor discharge guide.

steps.text: Look for damage: domed or split tops, bulging bottoms, brown crust or wet residue around the legs, a capacitor pushed up off the board, or a cracked or swollen run capacitor case. Any of these means replace it.
Read the label: capacitance (µF, nF or pF), voltage, and tolerance (such as ±5% or ±10%). Dual run capacitors have two values and three terminals marked C (common), FAN and HERM (compressor).
Free at least one leg from the circuit before measuring. Other parts on the board change the reading.
steps.warn: Desoldering irons run at over 300 °C. Rest the iron in a stand.

steps.text: Set the meter to capacitance (a capacitor symbol, or F). Touch the probes to the terminals, red to + on electrolytics, and wait for the reading to settle.
Compare the reading with the label. Run capacitors should be within their printed tolerance, usually ±5–6%. Small electrolytics are often ±20%. Below that, the capacitor is drying out.

No capacitance setting? Use ohms. On a discharged electrolytic, the reading should start low and climb steadily to very high or OL as the meter charges it. Stuck near zero means shorted. OL at once on a large capacitor means open.
On metal-can run capacitors, measure from each terminal to the can. It should read OL.
Discharge again after testing, and label good ones with their measured value.

notes:
## Reading values

- 1 µF (microfarad) = 1,000 nF (nanofarads) = 1,000,000 pF (picofarads).
- Small ceramic and film capacitors use a three-digit code: two digits then the number of zeros, in pF. 104 = 10 followed by 4 zeros = 100,000 pF = 100 nF = 0.1 µF. 473 = 47 nF.
- A letter after the code gives tolerance: J = ±5%, K = ±10%, M = ±20%.

## Choosing a replacement

- Voltage rating: the same or higher, never lower.
- Capacitance: the same, or close to it. For motor run capacitors, match the µF within a few percent.
- Type: run capacitors must be run-rated; start capacitors are only for short bursts and fail if left in circuit.
- Electrolytics have a polarity. Fitted backwards and powered, they can burst.

## ESR

Electrolytic capacitors can show the right capacitance and still fail, because their internal resistance (ESR) has risen. A normal meter can't measure ESR; an ESR meter can. Bulging tops and symptoms such as a power supply that whines, flickers or won't start point to high ESR.

## Supercapacitors

Most meters can't measure capacitors of a farad or more. Test a supercapacitor by charging it slowly through a resistor to below its rated voltage, then checking it holds the voltage over a few hours.

## Common mistakes

- Measuring in circuit.
- Testing a charged capacitor and blowing the meter.
- Fitting a replacement with a lower voltage rating.
- Fitting an electrolytic backwards.
